# docs_audit_report — June 6, 2026

## TL;DR (stranger's 30-second take)
I'd bounce immediately. The page is littered with broken template injections (literal `pytest` temporary paths rendered in the text), dense insider alphabet-soup, and suspiciously perfect numbers that make it look like an overfitted toy project rather than a robust production tool.

## TOP 3 PROBLEMS
1. Broken templating & leaked paths — Literal `pytest` file paths (`@.tmp-pytest/pytest-of-ianblenke/...`) are injected directly into benchmark headlines and CSS font links.

## DETAILED FINDINGS
### Bloat
- Results Section — 12 cards — 12 is way too many isolated benchmark claims for a stranger to process; cap at 4 headline claims.
- Blog Section — 7 cards — Takes up too much vertical space with internal operational notes; cap at 3 most relevant posts.

### Internal jargon
- Stats bar / Recent progress — "FoVer math step-errors (5-seed)", "dual-condition; architecture-only 0.8947" — Complete gibberish to a stranger.
- Evidence Grid — "PRM-BiasBench-style attacks", "IterativeSelfRepair (HumanEval-50, execute-feedback-retry)", "VeriCoT equation-style CoT fix", "CCTU constrained micro-benchmark" — Raw internal experiment terminology with no meaning outside the project.
- Blog titles/descriptions — "NTK", "arXiv:2601.18753 NTK" — Unexplained acronyms that alienate general readers.
- Capabilities — "Test-Time Compute (TTC) & PREM" — Defining an acronym just to immediately use it as a card title adds cognitive load.
- Live benchmark — "Qwen3.6-35B-A3B" — Unnecessarily specific model string.

### Per-milestone narrative
- Recent progress card — "Repinned from v2 0.9857 after pre-submission adversarial audit; see Why We Report Two AUROCs Now." — Reads exactly like an internal project status update or commit message rather than value proposition copy.

### Inconsistencies
- Claimed AUROC — "0.9131 AUROC" vs "v2 0.9857" vs "architecture-only 0.8947" vs "0.91 AUROC" vs "0.90 AUC" across different cards. Throwing too many different AUROC numbers for different tasks feels like metric-shopping and confuses the core claim.

### Missing essentials
- Who maintains it? — The footer just says "Ian Blenke · Carnot Project". There is no credibility anchor (company, lab, or specific community backing) explaining why a user should trust this tool over the hundreds of other LLM frameworks.

### Fabrication signals
- Live benchmark — "HumanEval pass ... 0% → 36%" — A 0% baseline is highly suspicious for a modern 35B model.
- Math extraction card — "GSM8K extraction TP rate: 0.5 → 1.0" — A 1.0 (100%) true positive rate is suspiciously perfect.
- Adversarial audit card — "k=5 ensemble catches 60/60 attacks" — 100% catch rate on a small sample size looks like overfitting.
- Blog: Dogfooding by the numbers — "Zero false positives" — Claiming 0 false positives on 639 experiments in constraint-based code analysis is unbelievable.

## WHAT'S WORKING
- The one-sentence summary "Catch the reasoning errors your LLM states with total confidence." is strong and clear.
- The 3-step "Extract -> Check -> Repair" breakdown is very easy to understand.
- The quickstart code blocks for Python and Rust show immediate, concrete usage.

2. Rewrite the "Recent Progress" card to use plain English instead of milestone/audit jargon and remove the internal narrative.

5. Consolidate the AUROC claims into a single, well-explained metric to avoid the appearance of metric-shopping.
